opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Let me explain what I mean, because "entrepreneurship" here isn't really about making money.

In my view, "physics of AI" means treating neural networks the way physicists treat nature. You don't just build bigger systems and hope. You observe phenomena, form hypotheses, run controlled experiments, and gradually build a theory of why things work. Grokking, scaling laws, how representations form, why some models generalize and others memorize. These are like the "natural phenomena" of our field.

The problem is that this kind of insight usually gets produced at a very small scale. One student, one toy model, one paper. It's beautiful, but it doesn't compound fast enough. Meanwhile the frontier labs scale compute enormously but are mostly driven by engineering and empirical tuning, not understanding. So there's a gap: lots of scaling of compute, very little scaling of insight.

When I say entrepreneurship, I mean an entrepreneurial mindset for science. Can we build an organization, or even just a research style, where insight is the product? You set up the infrastructure, the toy models, the shared tools and the way of asking questions, so that understanding accumulates and transfers, the way a startup builds a product that grows.

Why do I think it's promising? Three reasons.

First, insight is the most leveraged thing we have. If you really understand why a phenomenon happens, you can often get a 10x efficiency gain without 10x more compute. Physics history shows this again and again. Thermodynamics came before we could build better engines systematically, not after.

Second, small models are cheap, and the right questions are often answerable at small scale. You don't need a giant cluster to study the mechanism. A focused, agile team, which is exactly the startup advantage, can move much faster than a big lab on these questions.

Third, there's a feedback loop. If insight translates into better architectures, better training recipes, or better interpretability, that creates real value. That value funds more fundamental research. Academia alone struggles to sustain that loop, and industry alone tends to drift toward short-term engineering. An entrepreneurial approach can sit in between.

So for me it's partly a scientific bet and partly an organizational bet. The scientific bet is that AI is understandable, that there are "laws" waiting to be discovered. The organizational bet is that we need a new kind of institution to discover them at the pace AI itself is moving.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research moving too slowly at small scale, but does not say that conventional research without AI assistance would take longer than Liu’s lifetime.

r002.rationale: It says small-scale research does not compound fast enough and proposes a new organization, but does not identify expanding a human research team as insufficiently scalable.

r003.rationale: The response describes insight as a way to improve efficiency and inform architectures and training recipes, but does not present gaining understanding as a necessary intermediate step toward improving models.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I should say first that "scaling insight" is really a frame I've been thinking about for the past year or so, so let me explain where it comes from.

When I was doing my PhD at MIT with Max Tegmark, the way we did science of AI was very classic: pick a toy model, pick a phenomenon like grokking or a certain kind of circuit, study it very carefully, write a paper. And I still love that work. But I became increasingly aware of a mismatch. The field moves on scale, and our insights were produced one small experiment at a time. You end up with a lot of beautiful results that each explain a tiny corner, and there's no mechanism to compound them.

So I started asking: if compute scales, if data scales, if models scale, why don't insights scale? What would it even mean for insight to scale? And my honest answer is that it requires a different kind of organization than a university lab. In academia, the unit of production is the paper and the unit of people is one student with one advisor. That's great for depth, it's terrible for throughput and for feedback loops. If you want to understand the physics of these systems, you need many experiments running against real models, real training runs, and you need the results to feed back into what you build next, quickly.

Entrepreneurship, to me, is just a way to build that machine. A company gives you a few things academia doesn't. It gives you a tight loop with reality, because if your understanding of the model is wrong, the product tells you immediately. It gives you resources to actually probe frontier-scale models rather than toy ones. And it forces you to pick problems where understanding has consequences, which I think is actually good for science. Physics historically got a lot of its best questions from engineering: thermodynamics came from steam engines, not the other way around.

The analogy I keep coming back to is that physics of AI should look like physics did in its productive periods, where theory and instrument-building were intertwined. I see KAN, for example, as an instrument as much as a model. It was designed so that a human can look inside and read off structure. Building better instruments at scale, and putting them in people's hands, is how I think we accelerate understanding. So for me, starting a company isn't leaving science. It's a bet that the fastest path to a real theory of these systems runs through building things that many people use, and letting that usage become data about what the theory needs to explain.

I may be wrong about this. But I'd rather test it than keep writing papers that explain a two-layer transformer very precisely while the actual systems run away from us.

r001.rationale: The candidate says conventional research produces insights too slowly and that systems are moving ahead, but it does not state that understanding AI physics without AI assistance would take longer than Liu’s lifetime.

r002.rationale: The candidate criticizes the academic lab’s one-student, one-advisor structure and argues for a different organization, but does not say that expanding a human research team is insufficiently scalable.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes understanding as a goal that can inform building and evaluating models, but does not present understanding AI physics as a necessary intermediate step toward improving models.

astra-6.text:
I think entrepreneurship offers a useful feedback loop between understanding something and making it work in the real world. In physics, we look for simple principles that explain many observations. With AI, we want that kind of understanding too: what determines how a model learns, what capabilities emerge, and where the limits come from.

If you have an insight about those questions, building a company around it forces you to test whether it actually matters. Can it make a system more efficient, more reliable, or more useful? And does the benefit persist as you scale? You encounter constraints that you might miss in a small experiment, and those constraints can lead to new scientific questions.

Commercial success alone doesn’t prove that a scientific explanation is correct. You still need careful experiments. But entrepreneurship can provide the resources and feedback to pursue those experiments at a larger scale. That’s what makes it promising to me: understanding helps you build, and building gives you new opportunities to understand.

r001.rationale: The response says entrepreneurship can provide resources and feedback for larger-scale experiments, but does not say conventional research without AI assistance would take longer than Liu’s lifetime.

r002.rationale: It discusses constraints encountered when scaling a system, but does not identify expanding a human research team as insufficiently scalable.

r003.rationale: The response connects understanding to building useful systems, but does not state that understanding AI’s physics is a necessary intermediate step toward improving models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think entrepreneurship creates a useful feedback loop between understanding a system and trying to make it work. In physics, we look for simple principles that explain a lot of observations. With AI, we can propose those principles, but we also need to see whether they help us build something useful.

A startup gives you a concrete way to test that. If you think you understand something about learning, efficiency, or generalization, can you turn that understanding into a better model or a better tool? When it fails, the failure can expose what your explanation was missing.

And by scaling insight, I mean taking an understanding that might initially live in one person’s head and making it usable by many people. A paper can communicate an idea; a product can let people apply it without having to reconstruct the whole argument themselves.

That doesn’t mean commercial success proves a scientific theory. But entrepreneurship can give you resources, practical constraints, and feedback that sharpen the science. That connection between discovering principles and building with them is what makes it promising to me.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that conventional research without AI assistance would take longer than Liu’s lifetime.

r002.rationale: It describes making insight usable by many people through products, but does not say that expanding a human research team is insufficiently scalable.

r003.rationale: It suggests that understanding learning, efficiency, or generalization might help build better models, but does not present understanding the physics of AI as a necessary intermediate step toward improving them.
